metaDescription: We evaluated six SDS-Plus rotary hammer drills, cordless and corded, on joules, motor, vibration control, modes and bit capacity for concrete work.
expertTake: The Milwaukee M18 brushless D-handle rotary hammer is our best overall pick because it pairs brushless efficiency, the AVS anti-vibration system and a battery platform with a long tool list. The ENEACRO 13 amp corded unit is the value pick for heavy concrete work, with 7.4 joules claimed and six speeds. Anyone who only drills a few holes in masonry a year should skip a rotary hammer and use a standard hammer drill.
introParagraphs: A rotary hammer drill is the tool for real concrete. Unlike a regular hammer drill, which rattles the bit with a clutch, a rotary hammer uses a piston mechanism that delivers a powerful, controlled blow while the bit turns, so it drills holes quickly in masonry and can switch to chiselling mode for light demolition.

The details that matter are impact energy in joules, motor type, the SDS-Plus chuck and how well the tool controls vibration. Cordless models have closed the gap with corded ones for small holes, but corded units still lead on sustained heavy work.

products.name: Milwaukee M18 Brushless 1 Inch SDS-Plus D-Handle Rotary Hammer

specList.label: Runtime claim
specList.value: Up to 100 holes of 3/8 by 2 inch per charge, with an XC5.0 battery

products.description:
The Milwaukee M18 brushless rotary hammer is a 1 inch SDS-Plus D-handle model that the maker says drills 3/8 by 2 inch holes faster than corded 1 inch D-handle rotary hammers and can manage up to 100 holes per charge with an M18 XC5.0 battery. The AVS anti-vibration system reduces vibration at the handles, which matters when you drill overhead into concrete for hours.

The tradeoff is cost and the maker's claim. The cut counts depend on the battery and the hole size, and a cordless unit is expensive once you add batteries. Compared with the ENEACRO corded model, the Milwaukee has less raw impact energy but far more convenience and lower vibration. It suits electricians, HVAC installers and contractors already on the M18 platform.

Keep the chuck clean and lightly greased, check the dust boot if fitted and use sharp carbide-tipped SDS-Plus bits. Wear a respirator rated for silica dust, eye and ear protection, and let the tool cool when drilling large numbers of holes.
products.bestFor: Electricians and installers who want a cordless, low-vibration SDS-Plus hammer.
pros: Brushless motor extends runtime and cuts heat
AVS anti-vibration system reduces hand fatigue overhead
Maker quotes up to 100 holes of 3/8 by 2 inch per charge
Shares batteries with the large M18 tool range
cons: Costs far more than corded units once batteries are added
Impact energy is lower than heavy corded 1-1/4 inch models

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX 1 Inch D-Handle Cordless Rotary Hammer, 2.6J
products.description:
The DEWALT 20V MAX D-handle rotary hammer is a 1 inch SDS-Plus cordless unit with a brushless motor and a 2.6 joule optimised mechanism that the maker says drills faster than corded equivalents. The electronics hold speed through the application so the tool does not bog down, and DEWALT describes the mechanism as German engineered.

The tradeoff is power class. A 2.6 joule cordless hammer is a precision drilling tool for small to medium holes, not a demolition tool. Compared with the Milwaukee M18, the DEWALT is similar in class and platform strength, and the choice often comes down to which battery system you already own. It suits electricians, plumbers and remodelers drilling anchors and conduit holes.

Clean and lightly grease the chuck, store batteries indoors and use SDS-Plus bits designed for hammer use. Always wear a dust mask and eye protection, and use a depth stop where it is fitted.
products.bestFor: Contractors on the DEWALT platform who drill anchors and conduit holes.
pros: Brushless motor with electronics that maintain speed under load
Two point six joule mechanism handles small to medium holes quickly
D-handle gives control for overhead and vertical drilling
Shares batteries with the DEWALT 20V MAX range
cons: Not a demolition tool and limited for large holes
Cordless price rises once batteries and charger are added

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX SDS Rotary Hammer DCH273B, 2.1J
products.description:
The DEWALT DCH273B is a lighter SDS cordless rotary hammer with 2.1 joules of impact energy, three application modes and an active vibration control system that reduces vibration at the handles. It is sold as a bare tool, and the listing says its light weight suits rod hanging and seismic anchors.

The tradeoff is power. At 2.1 joules it is a step below the 2.6 joule DEWALT and far below corded models, so it is a precision tool for small holes. Compared with the 2.6 joule D-handle, the DCH273B is a pistol-grip style that is lighter and easier to hold overhead but cannot match the drilling speed. It suits electricians and installers who spend hours with the tool above their head.

Charge batteries ahead of the job, keep the chuck clean and use quality SDS-Plus bits. Wear a respirator and eye protection.
products.bestFor: Electricians and installers who drill overhead all day and value low weight.
pros: Light weight reduces fatigue on overhead anchor work
Active vibration control cuts the shock at the handles
Three modes cover drilling, hammer drilling and chiselling
Compatible with the DEWALT 20V MAX battery range
cons: Two point one joules limits it to small and medium holes
Sold as a bare tool, so batteries and charger cost extra

products.name: ENEACRO 1-1/4 Inch SDS-Plus 13 Amp Rotary Hammer, 7.4J

specList.label: Capacity
specList.value: Up to 1-1/4 inch holes in concrete

products.description:
The ENEACRO is a corded 1-1/4 inch SDS-Plus rotary hammer with a 13 amp, 1500 watt copper motor that the listing says delivers 5.5 ft-lbs, or about 7.4 joules, of impact energy, a six-speed variable dial and four modes that let it drill, hammer drill, chisel and position the chisel. It is aimed at heavy concrete work and light demolition.

The tradeoff is that the joule figure is a maker claim, and brand support and spare parts are less established than DEWALT or Milwaukee. Compared with the Milwaukee M18, the ENEACRO delivers far more raw impact energy for far less money, but it is heavier, has a cord and has less refined vibration control. It suits owners with large holes and demolition jobs who do not mind a cord.

Keep the vents clear, grease the chuck, inspect the cord and replace brushes when they wear. Use a respirator for concrete dust.
products.bestFor: Heavy concrete drilling and light demolition at a gentle tier.
pros: Thirteen amp copper motor delivers strong claimed impact energy
Six-speed dial allows control for different bits and materials
Four modes include chiselling for light demolition
Handles holes up to 1-1/4 inch in concrete
cons: Joule figure is a maker claim, not independently verified
Heavy and corded, with less refined vibration control

products.name: DongCheng 1-1/8 Inch SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer, 9.2A, 3.6J
products.description:
The DongCheng is a corded 1-1/8 inch SDS-Plus rotary hammer with a 9.2 amp, 1100 watt motor, 3.6 joules of impact energy at 5,000 blows per minute and a dual-mode design that switches between rotary hammer and chisel. A built-in mechanical safety clutch disengages the drive if the bit jams, which spares wrists. The kit includes drill bits and chisels.

The tradeoff is power and platform. A 3.6 joule unit is a step below the 13 amp models, so it drills smaller holes in concrete more slowly, and the brand has limited service in some markets. Compared with the ENEACRO, the DongCheng is lighter and cheaper, but less capable on large holes. It suits homeowners and light contractors drilling anchors and removing tiles.

Check the safety clutch before each job, keep vents clear and use sharp SDS-Plus bits. Wear a dust mask and eye protection, and clean the chuck regularly.
products.bestFor: Homeowners and light contractors who need an affordable corded SDS hammer.
pros: Three point six joules handles anchors and light chiselling
Mechanical safety clutch protects against bit jams
Kit includes bits and chisels to start immediately
Lighter and cheaper than 13 amp heavy models
cons: Slower on large holes than 13 amp rotary hammers
Brand support and spare parts are less widespread

products.name: AOBEN 13 Amp 1-1/4 Inch SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer

specList.label: Modes
specList.value: Hammer only, hammer drill, drill only

products.description:
The AOBEN is a corded 1-1/4 inch SDS-Plus rotary hammer with a 13 amp, 1500 watt motor, three modes (hammer only for chiselling, hammer drill and drill only), a rubber 360 degree adjustable handle and a safety clutch with vibration control. The listing positions it as a heavy-duty demolition and drilling tool.

The tradeoff is refinement and verification. Listings give less detail on impact energy and the vibration system than Milwaukee or DEWALT, and brand support is thinner. Compared with the ENEACRO, the AOBEN is similar in class, so the choice often comes down to availability. It suits users who want a 13 amp tool for concrete at an easy tier.

Keep the chuck greased, check the cord and brushes, and use quality bits. Wear a respirator and ear protection.
products.bestFor: Concrete drilling and demolition at the lowest cost for 13 amp power.
pros: Thirteen amp motor delivers strong power for large holes
Three modes include hammer-only chiselling

buyingCriteria.explanation: Impact energy, measured in joules, describes how hard each blow hits. A 2 to 3 joule cordless unit handles anchors and conduit holes, while 5 to 8 joules suits large holes and chiselling. Joule claims on off-brand tools are often optimistic, so compare similar brands only.

Corded 13 amp models, like the ENEACRO, deliver sustained heavy power. Cordless models, like the Milwaukee M18 and DEWALT 20V, give mobility and are fast on small holes. Choose cordless for installers and corded for large holes and demolition.

SDS-Plus is a bit system that lets the bit slide in the chuck so the hammer action drives it. A 1 inch capacity covers most anchor work, while 1-1/4 inch units handle larger core holes. Do not use regular round-shank bits.

Vibration builds up quickly when drilling concrete. Systems like Milwaukee's AVS and DEWALT's active vibration control reduce hand fatigue. Look for rubber handles and side handles that suit your grip.
Most rotary hammers offer drill only, hammer drill and chisel modes. A safety clutch disengages when the bit jams, protecting your wrist. Check that the mode selector is positive and does not slip.

Drilling concrete produces silica dust, which is hazardous. Use a dust shroud or vacuum, wear a respirator rated for silica and eye and ear protection. Dust and noise are the real long-term risks of this tool.

specDecoder.meaning: The energy of each hammer blow. A rotary hammer is about energy per blow, not blows per minute alone.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEWALT lists 2.6 and 2.1 joules, the DongCheng 3.6 and the ENEACRO claims 7.4.

specDecoder.meaning: How many hammer blows occur each minute. Higher BPM gives more blows but not always more energy.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DongCheng lists 5,000 BPM, which is typical of mid-power rotary hammers.

specDecoder.meaning: A quick-change bit system with a slotted shank that lets the bit move axially so the hammer can strike it.
specDecoder.watchFor: All the tools here use SDS-Plus, so use SDS-Plus bits only.

specDecoder.meaning: Current draw of a corded motor, a rough indicator of power. A 13 amp motor is near the 15 amp limit of a household circuit.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ENEACRO and AOBEN are 13 amp, and the DongCheng is 9.2 amp.

specDecoder.meaning: Systems that isolate the handle from the hammer mechanism to reduce vibration reaching your hands.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Milwaukee lists AVS, and the DEWALT lists shocks active vibration control.

howWeEvaluated.title: Impact energy and power
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared joule ratings, motor amps and platform class from published specifications. The ENEACRO claims the most, and the cordless units sit lower. We treated off-brand joule claims with caution.

howWeEvaluated.title: Vibration and comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at anti-vibration systems, handle design and weight. The Milwaukee AVS and DEWALT vibration control earned credit. Rubber handles and side handles were rated for comfort.

howWeEvaluated.title: Chuck, modes and safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered SDS-Plus capacity, mode selectors and safety clutches. The DongCheng's clutch and the AOBEN's three modes stood out. We noted that every rotary hammer needs dust protection.

howWeEvaluated.title: Corded versus cordless fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched tools to realistic users, using owner feedback patterns on runtime and weight. Cordless suits installers, corded suits heavy holes. We rated runtime claims as maker figures.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We asked what each extra cost buys in platform, support or power. The Milwaukee and DEWALT carry platform value, and off-brand units offer power for less. We judged by fit rather than raw joules.

cards.text: A 13 amp tool like the ENEACRO delivers sustained power for large holes and chiselling at a lower cost.

cards.label: Cordless

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for demolition and large holes, and cordless for installation and mobility.

cards.text: Light weight, low vibration and a battery platform you already own. Overhead work punishes heavy tools.

maintenance.why: Concrete dust wears the chuck and bits. A light grease keeps bits sliding freely.
Dull bits slow the work and strain the motor. Only use SDS-Plus bits made for hammer action.
Worn brushes weaken corded motors, and nicked cords are a hazard. Replace them promptly.
Concrete dust clogs vents and overheats the motor. Compressed air keeps them clear.
Cold and heat shorten battery life. Store at partial charge in a dry place.

faq.q: What is the difference between a rotary hammer and a hammer drill?
faq.a: A rotary hammer uses a piston mechanism that delivers a strong blow, which is much more effective in concrete. A hammer drill uses a ratcheting clutch that is fine for brick and light masonry. A good rule is to match the tool to the biggest hole you drill regularly rather than the biggest it can manage, because a tool that is too heavy gets left in the van and a tool that is too light stalls and wears out.

faq.q: How much should I spend on a rotary hammer?
faq.a: A corded model costs the least, while cordless tools on a platform cost more with batteries. Spend according to how much concrete you drill.

faq.q: How long does a rotary hammer last?
faq.a: A quality tool can last many years with care. Brushes, the chuck and bits are the wear items, and dust is the main enemy.

faq.q: Does more joules mean a better tool?
faq.a: Not always. More energy suits large holes and chiselling, but it also means a heavier tool. For anchors, 2 to 3 joules is plenty. Anchors and conduit holes rarely need more than three joules, and chasing a big number mostly adds weight and cost. Look for a decent chuck, low vibration and a platform you already own before comparing joule claims.
Yes, it contains silica, which is hazardous to breathe. Use a dust shroud or vacuum, wear a respirator rated for silica, and wear eye and ear protection.

faq.q: Can I use a rotary hammer as a regular drill?
faq.a: Yes, in drill-only mode with SDS-Plus bits or a chuck adapter, but they are heavy and not ideal for fine work. A regular drill is better for wood and metal. If you have only a few holes to drill, hiring a rotary hammer for a day usually costs less than buying one and works better than forcing a standard drill through concrete.
